title: Evaluating the Quality of Higher Education Instructor-Constructed Multiple-Choice Tests: Impact on Student Grades https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2017.00024/full
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 11, 2025 — original paper:
summary: This entry captures Barton's summary of Brown and Abdulnabi's 2017 study assessing 100 instructor-written multiple-choice questions from a higher-education midterm and final exam using both classical test theory and item response theory. The analysis found significant quality problems in the instructor-constructed items, and showed that the two-parameter logistic IRT model produced more accurate estimates of student ability than raw scores — with real consequences for pass/fail decisions. The paper argues that most higher-education instructors lack training in psychometrics, so statistical item analysis (not just judgment) is necessary to catch items that are too easy, too hard, guessable, or fail to discriminate between strong and weak students. It closes by proposing automated item-analysis systems to help time-poor instructors apply this rigor without needing to become psychometricians themselves.
points: Poorly constructed multiple-choice items — not poor teaching — can produce misleading conclusions about what students actually know, directly affecting pass/fail decisions.
Statistical item analysis (checking difficulty, discrimination, and distractor effectiveness) should supplement instructor judgment, because flawed items aren't always obvious just from reading them.
The two-parameter logistic IRT model outperformed simpler models (Rasch/1PL, 3PL) at fitting this dataset, suggesting instructors shouldn't assume one 'default' scoring model is always appropriate.
Because most higher-ed instructors lack psychometric training, automated item-analysis tools could make this level of rigor practically achievable without demanding new expertise.
quotes: The authors assessed 100 MCQs from a midterm and final exam using Classical Test Theory (CTT) and Item Response Theory (IRT) models, finding significant issues with item quality.
Poorly constructed items, rather than poor teaching or learning, can result in inappropriate decisions about student ability and give inappropriate feedback to both students and instructors.

Items that are too easy or too difficult, easy to guess, or that do not positively discriminate between high and low performing students should be removed. This is especially important because the statistical analysis can identify problems that may not be apparent to the teacher.

Given that most higher education teachers lack training in psychometrics, automated item analysis systems would be beneficial, and such systems should allow the teacher to make decisions about which items to remove.
The inclusion of poor quality items can have an impact on students' overall course grades and on pass/fail decisions.
The overwhelming conclusion is that item statistical analysis is a necessary adjunct to judgment-based evaluation of item quality in MCQ testing in higher education
